questions.question: Which statement is the best example of a problem representation?
choices: Chest pain
A 64-year-old with diabetes has new exertional substernal pressure relieved by rest and associated dyspnea
Order an ECG and troponin
The patient probably has GERD
questions.explanation: A problem representation concisely summarizes discriminating features, context, and trajectory without prematurely naming the diagnosis.

questions.question: What should occur before a detailed outpatient diagnostic workup?
choices: Assess physiologic stability, vital signs, mental status, perfusion, and emergency red flags
Order the broadest laboratory panel available
Choose the most common diagnosis
Ask only about duration of symptoms
questions.explanation: Stability and time-sensitive emergencies come first. Instability can change the appropriate setting from outpatient workup to emergency evaluation.

questions.question: Which differential-diagnosis approach is safest for an FNP?
choices: List only the most likely diagnosis
Prioritize common causes, dangerous causes that must not be missed, and patient-specific causes
Include every disease in the textbook
Use a prior diagnosis without reassessment
questions.explanation: A prioritized differential links probability with consequence and patient-specific risk, guiding safe testing and disposition.

questions.question: What is the key diagnostic-stewardship question before ordering a test?
choices: Will this test produce the most numbers?
What diagnosis am I considering, and how would a result change management?
Can I order the test without speaking to the patient?
Will the result always provide a diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tests should answer a clinical question. Consider how results, false results, cost, harm, timing, and follow-up will affect management.

questions.question: Why does pretest probability matter when interpreting a diagnostic test?
choices: It changes how much a positive or negative result should change concern for disease
It makes all tests equally accurate
It eliminates the need for history and examination
It guarantees that a negative result rules out disease
questions.explanation: The meaning of a test result depends on clinical context. A low-probability positive may be false, and a negative result may not exclude disease when concern remains high.

questions.question: A clinician continues to treat a patient as having a viral illness despite new hypoxemia and pleuritic chest pain. Which cognitive pitfall is most relevant?
choices: Anchoring and premature closure
Shared decision-making
Diagnostic stewardship
Problem representation
questions.explanation: Anchoring fixes attention on an early impression; premature closure stops reassessment. New discordant findings should trigger a revised differential.

questions.question: Which documentation is most useful after a focused respiratory examination?
choices: Normal examination
Speaking in full sentences, no accessory muscle use, stable oxygen saturation at rest, and lungs clear to auscultation
Patient seems fine
No concerns
questions.explanation: Precise positive and meaningful negative findings show how the examination addressed the differential; a generic normal exam does not.

questions.question: A stable outpatient test is ordered. Which action is part of closing the diagnostic loop?
choices: Assume the portal message is sufficient for every result
Track the result, communicate it in understandable language, document action, and ensure needed follow-up occurs
Wait for the patient to call only if symptoms continue
Delete the order after the visit
questions.explanation: Diagnostic safety includes tracking, reviewing, communicating, and acting on results and referrals—not simply ordering them.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a safety net for outpatient care?
choices: A vague instruction to return if worse
Specific symptoms and time frames for calling, urgent reassessment, or emergency evaluation, plus a plan for results
A promise that the diagnosis is certain
Avoiding follow-up so the patient does not worry
questions.explanation: A safety net makes uncertainty manageable by defining what to monitor, when to act, who owns results, and how to obtain help.

questions.question: A patient has worsening unilateral calf swelling after immobility despite a reported negative initial study. What is the best FNP reasoning step?
choices: Assume the diagnosis is excluded permanently
Verify the test type, timing, adequacy, and current stability; reassess the differential and escalate as appropriate
Treat only the swelling with rest
Ignore new symptoms because one result was negative
questions.explanation: When the clinical course does not fit, reassess rather than allowing one result to replace clinical judgment. Test timing and type matter.
